spoken: At three thousand revolutions a minute, a car engine's crankshaft turns fifty times a second.
And yet each cylinder only burns fuel 25 times a second, which is once every two turns.
Its piston makes four trips for every burn, and only one of those trips actually pushes.
That's four trips for one push. It sounds wasteful.
It does. And it's still the design inside most car engines.
It's the four-stroke cycle. It was first patented by a man who never built one,
and made to work by a former grocery salesman, who later lost his patent.
Let's open one up. This is a simplified diagram of a single cylinder.
So inside the cylinder there's a piston, sliding up and down.
And a connecting rod links that piston to the crankshaft, which turns.
So up-and-down becomes round-and-round.
Exactly. Up top there are two valves. One lets air and fuel in, and the other lets burnt gas out.
And cams on a camshaft push them open, then springs close them again.
Between them sits the spark plug.
The piston's highest point is called top dead centre, and its lowest is called bottom dead centre.
At each of them the piston is momentarily at rest, before it turns around.
And one trip between them, up or down, is a stroke.
Now watch the piston as the crank turns. It follows along, but not in a perfectly even rhythm.
It looks like a smooth wave to me.
Nearly. But after a quarter turn, the piston has already covered more than half its stroke.

The rod tilts. That makes the piston hurry through the top half of the stroke, and dawdle through the bottom.
Okay. Let's run one whole cycle, slowly, from the top.
Stroke one is intake. The intake valve opens, and the falling piston draws in air and fuel.
It's pulled in by the partial vacuum it leaves behind.
Stroke 2 is compression. Both valves shut, and the rising piston squeezes the mixture into about a tenth of the space.
And by now the crankshaft has turned once, all the way round.
Near the top, the spark plug fires, and the mixture starts to burn.
Stroke three is power. The hot, high-pressure gas drives the piston down.
And that's the only stroke that pushes on the crank.
The other three just get the gas in, ready, and out again.
Stroke 4 is exhaust. The exhaust valve opens, and the rising piston pushes the burnt gas out.
Then it all starts again. That's four strokes, two turns of the crank, and one push.
That's why the camshaft turns at half the crankshaft's speed, so that each valve opens once per cycle.
So it's two turns of the crank for one turn of the cam.
But what carries the piston through the three strokes that don't push?
It's a heavy flywheel. It soaks up energy from each power stroke, and gives some back to squeeze the next charge.
So who came up with all this? The idea is older than the engine that made it famous.
In 1860, Étienne Lenoir in Paris built a gas engine that burned its fuel without compressing it first.
And it turned only about four percent of the fuel's energy into work.
Four percent. So almost all of it went to waste.
Almost all. Then a travelling salesman in Germany, Nicolaus Otto, learned of it, and started building engines himself.
In 1862 he tried one that compressed its charge first. It ran for a few minutes, then destroyed itself.
That same year, in France, Alphonse Beau de Rochas patented the four-stroke cycle. But he never built an engine.
So the idea existed on paper before anyone made it run.
Meanwhile, in eighteen sixty-four, Otto and Eugen Langen founded the first company devoted to making engines.
Their atmospheric engine won a gold medal at the 1867 Paris World's Fair, at about 12 percent efficiency.
That's three times Lenoir's.
Then, in 1876, Otto's company built an engine that compressed its charge in four strokes.
It was an immediate success, and the first commercially successful engine to compress its charge in the cylinder.
And two of Otto's former engineers, Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, made it small and fast enough for vehicles.
But in eighteen eighty-six the patent was cancelled in Germany, because Beau de Rochas had patented the cycle first.
So a patent for an engine nobody had built ended Otto's monopoly.
And neither Otto nor Daimler had even known that patent existed.
Still, the engines spread. By 1889, more than 50 companies were building Otto-type engines.
And the cycle still carries Otto's name. It's called the Otto cycle.
So why does squeezing first help so much? Engineers answer with a graph of pressure against volume.

During intake, the volume grows, at about the pressure outside.
During compression, the volume shrinks tenfold, and the pressure climbs steeply.

During the power stroke, the hot gas expands and pushes, and its pressure falls.
At the bottom, the exhaust valve opens, and the pressure drops back.
During exhaust, the piston sweeps the gas out, and the loop closes.

The area inside it is the net work, which is what the power stroke gave, minus what the compression cost.
So squeezing costs some work, but the hot gas pays back much more on the way down.

Sixty percent? Car engines don't get anywhere near that.
No. Real engines lose energy to heat and friction along the way. A petrol engine turns about thirty percent into useful work.
But the lesson holds. If you squeeze harder, you get more work from the same fuel.
So why do most petrol car engines stop at around eight to twelve to one?
Because squeezing a gas heats it, and a hot enough mixture can ignite by itself.
Normally, the spark starts a flame front that sweeps across the chamber.
But if the unburnt mixture ahead of the flame gets too hot, pockets of it explode all at once.
That's called knock. It causes a metallic pinging, and pressure spikes that can damage the engine.
So it's knock, not the formula, that sets the limit.
Right. A fuel's octane rating measures how well it resists igniting by itself. Higher octane allows more squeeze.

Before the piston has even finished squeezing?

The valves are early, too. They open before the end of a stroke, and close after it.

That's valve overlap, and it's designed in on purpose.
Why would you want both open?
The outgoing exhaust is moving fast, and it helps draw the fresh charge in behind it.
So the trick is to close the exhaust valve just as the fresh charge reaches it.
Exactly. Racing engines use lots of overlap. Road engines, which must idle smoothly below a thousand revolutions a minute, use less.
And many now shift their camshafts as they run, to get both power at high revs and a smooth idle.
One cylinder gives one push every two turns. That's a lumpy way to drive a car.
